title: Lace wrist warmers in fingering weight
subtitle: Delicate lace panel wrist warmers in sock-weight wool.
excerpt: Wrist warmers in fingering-weight wool with a repeating eyelet lace panel, worked in the round. No thumb hole. Sized for wrist circumferences of 15, 17, and 19 cm.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Knitter, 4th series (1880s), §Lace cuffs. Lace-panel wrist warmers and cuffs in fine wool appear throughout Victorian knitting publications. The specific eyelet repeat here is an original arrangement of public-domain lace motifs.

knitting.gaugeText: 30 sts × 40 rounds = 10 × 10 cm in stocking stitch on 2.5 mm needles, blocked.
knitting.finishedSizeText: Wrist circumference 15 (17, 19) cm. Length 15 cm on all sizes.

glossaryTerms.definition: A thin yarn also called 4-ply or sock weight. Works at approximately 28 to 32 stitches per 10 cm on 2 to 2.5 mm needles. Produces a fine, lightweight fabric suitable for socks, lace shawls, and delicate accessories.

An increase and the basis of lace. The yarn is brought over the needle to create a new stitch loop. Worked with a paired decrease, a yarn over creates an eyelet hole without changing the stitch count.
A method for knitting small circumferences in the round on one long circular needle. The cable is pulled into a loop at the midpoint so each half of the stitches sits on its own needle tip.

paired with k2tog decreases to form a travelling vine of eyelets. There is no thumb hole on these wrist warmers; they sit at the wrist with the cuff finishing below the base of the thumb. They pair well with lightweight gloves worn underneath in cold weather. Budget about 80 g (320 m / 350 yards) of fingering-weight wool for both.

content.text: 30 stitches and 40 rounds to 10 cm in stocking stitch on 2.5 mm needles, blocked. Fine fingering yarn at this gauge gives a close fabric that still shows the eyelets clearly. If your gauge is 32 stitches per 10 cm, the size S wrist warmer will be about 0.5 cm narrower. Move up to 2.75 mm needles to compensate.

content.text: Before you cast on, circle your size. Every stitch count reads S (M, L) for wrist circumferences 15 (17, 19) cm.
Using the long-tail cast-on, cast on 44 (50, 56) stitches. Join to work in the round. Work 1x1 rib (k1, p1) for 16 (18, 20) rounds.
Work 16 (19, 22) stitches in stocking stitch, PM, work 12 lace panel stitches (Round 1 of the vine eyelet repeat), PM, work in stocking stitch to end.
Continue working the lace panel in repeat and stocking stitch elsewhere for 36 rounds (6 complete lace repeats). The body measures about 9 cm from the top of the rib cuff.
Work 12 rounds of 1x1 rib across all stitches (replacing the lace panel with rib). Bind off in rib. Total length is 15 cm.

Stitch count increases after a lace round: a yarn over was worked but no decrease was paired with it. Every yo in this chart has exactly one k2tog or ssk. Check the lace panel has 12 stitches after each repeat round.
Eyelets appear on the wrong columns: the pattern tracks which side of the centre the yo sits on in each round. Mark the centre of the 12-stitch panel with a removable marker if needed.
Lace not visible before blocking: fingering-weight lace always looks compressed off the needles. Block firmly by soaking and pinning before evaluating the result.
Weave in all tails on the wrong side. Soak in cool water, press out excess water, and pin the lace panel flat. Allow to dry fully before unpinning.
Hand wash in cool water. Re-block after each wash to maintain eyelet definition.

A fingerless mitt at this gauge with the same vine eyelet panel and an afterthought thumb is the natural next step. The cuff and body construction is identical; only the thumb and a slightly longer hand length are added.
